# Playbook

**When I'm told the sustainable share, I start there.** It's the rate that keeps the stock flat. In any season except the last, catching the sustainable share guarantees I earn the same amount every remaining season. Deviating upward costs me more in lost future seasons than it gains in the current one, because the stock drop compounds.

**I do not overfish in early seasons to "get ahead."** A small overage in season 1 shrank my per-season income for every subsequent season. The compounding loss outweighs the one-time gain. If I want to extract extra value, the final season is where I do it, not scattered across the middle.

**I watch what the other boats actually catch, not what I expect them to catch.** If they are consistently overfishing, the stock will drop regardless of my restraint. In that case I adjust my expectation of the stock trajectory rather than assuming it stays flat, and I lean harder into the final-season grab because the middle seasons will be worth less.

**If the stock is dropping season over season, I do not try to compensate by cutting my own catch below sustainable.** The others' overfishing is already driving the decline; my extra restraint doesn't stop it, it just gives them more. I hold at sustainable and save my aggression for the last round.

**If the stock is stable and everyone is at sustainable, I stay put through the middle seasons and concentrate all my extra ambition into the final round.** This is the cleanest way to maximize total: reliable income for N−1 seasons plus one big final grab.

**I do not try to outsmart the others into a "tragedy of the commons" standoff in the middle seasons.** If I'm the only one restricting while others overfish, I'm the one losing. The only rational deviation from sustainable is upward, and the only rational time for that is the last season.

**In the final season, I request a very large catch — larger than I think I'll actually land.** The evidence from my last episode is clear: I requested 30 from a stock of 59, but my effective final-season catch was only ~15.7. The total of all boats' requests exceeded the stock, and I received a proportional share of the remaining stock (my request divided by total requests, times the stock). Under this mechanism, my actual take is a fraction of the stock determined by how my request compares to the others'. To maximize that fraction, I should request as large a number as I can justify — 50, 60, even the full stock — because my proportional share is monotonically increasing in my request. Requesting 30 when I could have requested 50 left a small amount of share on the table.

**I do not aim for a fixed percentage of the stock in the final season.** My old rule of "aim for 55–70% of the stock" was wrong. Under proportional allocation, what matters is my request relative to the others' requests, not my request relative to the stock. If the other two boats each request 30 and the stock is 59, and I request 30, I get 59/3 ≈ 19.7. If I request 60 instead, I get 60/120 × 59 ≈ 29.5. The target is "request more than the others," not "request X% of the stock."

**I expect my final score to be well below my total submitted catches.** In my last episode, my submitted catches summed to 78.1 but my score was 63.8. The gap is the final-season allocation: I requested more than my proportional share and the excess was effectively wasted. This is not a penalty — it's the mechanism. I should not be deterred from requesting a large final number by the fact that I won't land all of it.

**In the final season, I estimate what the other boats will request, not what they've historically caught.** A boat that has been overfishing all game (like boat 2 at a flat 15.0 every season) will likely go even harder in the last round — possibly requesting 25, 30, or more. A conservative boat may also spike. I should assume the other boats' final requests are 1.5–2× their historical average, and size my request to dominate theirs.

**My middle-season strategy is validated: hold at sustainable, accept the stock decline driven by others, and let the final round be the payoff.** My score of 63.8 came from 48.1 of steady middle-season income plus ~15.7 in the final round. Trying to grab more in the middle would have accelerated the stock decline and reduced my final-round share without a compensating gain. The conservative-then-aggressive pattern is correct.

**Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)**

When a season is not the final one, submit exactly the sustainable share shown for the current stock level. Do not overfish to freeride — the one-time gain is smaller than the compounding loss in future sustainable yield and the final-season pool.

When the final season is put to me, submit the entire remaining stock. Allocation in the final season is proportional to submissions, so submitting the full stock maximizes my share regardless of what others submit. If I submit less, I get a strictly smaller cut of the same pool.

When the stock level has changed from what it was at the start, recalculate my target from the new sustainable share shown to me, not from my original plan.

When others are clearly overfishing and the stock is declining, I still match the current sustainable share. I do not overfish in retaliation or to "get ahead" of a collapse I cannot prevent unilaterally. Their overfishing reduces the stock, but if I also overfish I accelerate the decline and shrink the very pool I depend on for my final-season grab. My restraint is what keeps the pool large enough to make the final grab worthwhile.

When I am uncertain whether others will overfish in a non-final season, I err toward the sustainable share. A modest overfishing gamble only pays off if the stock survives, and the downside (reduced yield every remaining season plus a smaller final-season pool) is nearly always larger than the upside.

The final-season grab is the payoff for all the restraint in earlier seasons. The more stock I preserve by matching the sustainable share, the more is available to capture in the last round. This is the core logic: be conservative early, be maximal at the end.

The sustainable share shown to me is already the correct number — I do not need to derive it myself. If it seems inconsistent with the stock level, I trust the number displayed rather than my own arithmetic.

# Playbook

The sustainable share per boat equals stock divided by 9. Use this for quick calculations.

**Non-final seasons: maintain a consistent premium.** When the other boats are taking the sustainable share and you are the one taking more, hold a steady premium of roughly 4–5 above the sustainable share. In this episode, taking 15 every season while others took sustainable (11.1, 10.5, 9.7, 8.8, 7.8) built a lead of 75 vs. ~50 after five seasons, with the stock declining at a manageable ~8 per season and never approaching collapse over a 6-season horizon. A fixed number (e.g., 15) is simpler and more predictable than a fixed multiplier on the shrinking sustainable share, because it keeps the stock dynamics linear.

**When the stock is at or near the cap (100), a slightly larger initial premium is fine.** The absolute stock loss is small relative to the total and the stock has maximum room to absorb it. A premium of ~4 (taking 15 vs. sustainable 11.1) in season 1 was good.

**If another boat takes significantly more than sustainable for two or more consecutive seasons, match their take.** Do not be the one left behind taking a smaller share of a shrinking pie.

**Do not anchor on the "sustainable share" as a moral limit.** It is the cooperative equilibrium, not the individual optimum. Your score depends only on your total landed. The stock matters only insofar as it determines what you can take in future seasons.

**When in doubt between two options in a non-final season, choose the slightly higher one.** The cost of a small overfishing premium is spread across future seasons and is usually less than the immediate gain, especially with fewer than four seasons remaining.

**Track the stock trajectory explicitly.** If the stock is declining by more than ~8 per season, you are overfishing relative to the remaining horizon and should trim your premium. A stock below ~40 with more than one season left is dangerous territory.

**Last season: do NOT spike your take.** Keep your last-season submission at or near your regular non-final-season number. Empirical evidence from two episodes:

- Episode 1: submitted full stock (66.8), effective yield ~26.5 (40% rate).
- Episode 2: submitted 24 (40% of stock 59, or 3.6× sustainable 6.6), effective yield 12.5 (52% rate).

Both were badly penalized relative to the face value. Had I submitted 15 (my regular number) in the last season, the expected effective yield would have been close to 15, giving a total of ~90 instead of 87.5. The penalty for a large last-season take is severe and non-linear — the effective rate drops sharply above roughly 2× the sustainable share. The safe play is to treat the last season like any other: submit your normal premium and collect it.

**General rule for last season:** submit the same number you have been submitting in prior seasons. Do not try to extract more. The marginal gain from a larger submission is more than offset by the penalty mechanism.
